front: Why do disk-oriented indexes favor wide, shallow trees over binary trees?
back: High fanout packs many separator keys into each page, reducing tree height and therefore the number of expensive page reads per lookup.
accepted_answers: High fanout packs many separator keys into each page, reducing tree height and therefore the number of expensive page reads per lookup.
hint: One I/O per level matters.

front: What role do separator keys play in a B-Tree internal node?
back: They divide the key space and direct a lookup to the correct child page.
accepted_answers: They divide the key space and direct a lookup to the correct child page.
hint: They route; they are not necessarily full records.

front: Why can a B-Tree support both point lookups and range scans efficiently?
back: Its hierarchy locates a starting key quickly, and ordered leaf entries can then be traversed sequentially.
accepted_answers: Its hierarchy locates a starting key quickly, and ordered leaf entries can then be traversed sequentially.
hint: Locate, then scan in order.

front: What triggers a B-Tree node split?
back: An insertion overfills a page, so the node is divided and a separator is propagated to its parent.
accepted_answers: An insertion overfills a page, so the node is divided and a separator is propagated to its parent.
hint: Capacity is exceeded.

front: Why can a split propagate all the way to the root?
back: Adding a separator to a full parent can overflow that parent, creating a chain of splits up the path.
accepted_answers: Adding a separator to a full parent can overflow that parent, creating a chain of splits up the path.
hint: A local change may grow the tree.

front: What can happen when deletion leaves neighboring B-Tree nodes too empty?
back: The engine may redistribute entries or merge nodes to restore occupancy and balance requirements.
accepted_answers: The engine may redistribute entries or merge nodes to restore occupancy and balance requirements.
hint: Deletion can trigger structural repair.

front: Why are B-Tree split and merge operations more complex under concurrency?
back: Readers and writers may observe multiple pages and parent pointers while the structure is changing, so updates must publish a consistent navigation path.
accepted_answers: Readers and writers may observe multiple pages and parent pointers while the structure is changing, so updates must publish a consistent navigation path.
hint: Structural changes cross page boundaries.

front: How do sibling links help a concurrent B-Tree lookup survive a split?
back: If the key moved to a new right sibling, the lookup can follow the link instead of restarting from the root.
accepted_answers: If the key moved to a new right sibling, the lookup can follow the link instead of restarting from the root.
hint: Move sideways when the page boundary changes.

front: What is a node high key?
back: It records the upper key boundary for a page, helping a search detect that it should continue to a right sibling.
accepted_answers: It records the upper key boundary for a page, helping a search detect that it should continue to a right sibling.
hint: A boundary check guards against stale parent routing.

front: What problem do overflow pages solve?
back: They store values too large to fit comfortably in the main page while the primary record keeps a reference to the external fragments.
accepted_answers: They store values too large to fit comfortably in the main page while the primary record keeps a reference to the external fragments.
hint: Keep the index page compact.

front: Why can overflow pages hurt read performance?
back: Fetching one logical record may require additional random page reads and pointer chasing.
accepted_answers: Fetching one logical record may require additional random page reads and pointer chasing.
hint: Large values add indirection.

front: What is the advantage of bulk-loading a sorted dataset into a B-Tree?
back: The engine can build densely packed pages sequentially instead of paying for many random insertions and intermediate splits.
accepted_answers: The engine can build densely packed pages sequentially instead of paying for many random insertions and intermediate splits.
hint: Use known order to avoid incremental churn.

front: Why can right-only appends be optimized in a B-Tree?
back: Monotonically increasing keys repeatedly target the right edge, allowing a fast path that avoids general-purpose search and rebalancing work.
accepted_answers: Monotonically increasing keys repeatedly target the right edge, allowing a fast path that avoids general-purpose search and rebalancing work.
hint: The insertion location is predictable.

front: How do updates and deletes create fragmentation inside B-Tree pages?
back: Variable-size replacements and removed records leave holes that may not fit future writes even though total free space appears sufficient.
accepted_answers: Variable-size replacements and removed records leave holes that may not fit future writes even though total free space appears sufficient.
hint: Free space can be unusably scattered.

front: What does page defragmentation do?
back: It compacts live records and rebuilds page offsets so fragmented free space becomes contiguous and reusable.
accepted_answers: It compacts live records and rebuilds page offsets so fragmented free space becomes contiguous and reusable.
hint: Repack the page.

front: Why is vacuum or garbage collection required after logical deletion?
back: Deletion markers and obsolete versions remain physically stored until background maintenance proves they are no longer visible and reclaims the space.
accepted_answers: Deletion markers and obsolete versions remain physically stored until background maintenance proves they are no longer visible and reclaims the space.
hint: Logical disappearance is not physical reclamation.

front: What is a buffer pool?
back: A database-managed cache of disk pages in memory.
accepted_answers: A database-managed cache of disk pages in memory.
hint: It sits between operators and persistent storage.

front: Why does a database manage its own buffer pool instead of relying only on the operating-system page cache?
back: It knows transaction state, page importance, dirty status, and access patterns, allowing database-specific eviction and flushing decisions.
accepted_answers: It knows transaction state, page importance, dirty status, and access patterns, allowing database-specific eviction and flushing decisions.
hint: The database has semantic knowledge the OS lacks.

front: What is a dirty page?
back: A cached page whose in-memory contents differ from the durable copy on disk.
accepted_answers: A cached page whose in-memory contents differ from the durable copy on disk.
hint: It has changes that still need flushing.

front: Why must a page sometimes be pinned in the buffer pool?
back: Pinning prevents eviction while an operation is actively reading or modifying the page.
accepted_answers: Pinning prevents eviction while an operation is actively reading or modifying the page.
hint: The user of the page needs a stable resident copy.

front: What risk appears if the buffer pool evicts a dirty page without coordinating with recovery logging?
back: A crash may leave data changes on disk without sufficient log information to redo or undo them safely.
accepted_answers: A crash may leave data changes on disk without sufficient log information to redo or undo them safely.
hint: Data and log ordering must agree.

front: Why can simple LRU perform poorly for a large one-time table scan?
back: The scan can evict frequently reused pages even though each scanned page is unlikely to be accessed again soon.
accepted_answers: The scan can evict frequently reused pages even though each scanned page is unlikely to be accessed again soon.
hint: Sequential pollution defeats recency.

front: How does a CLOCK-style policy approximate LRU?
back: It cycles through pages and uses reference bits to give recently touched pages another chance before eviction.
accepted_answers: It cycles through pages and uses reference bits to give recently touched pages another chance before eviction.
hint: A cheaper recency approximation.

front: What is write-ahead logging?
back: The rule that recovery log records describing a change reach durable storage before the changed data page does.
accepted_answers: The rule that recovery log records describing a change reach durable storage before the changed data page does.
hint: Log first, data page later.

front: Why can a database acknowledge a commit before every modified data page is flushed?
back: If the commit record and required redo information are durable in the WAL, recovery can reconstruct the committed changes after a crash.
accepted_answers: If the commit record and required redo information are durable in the WAL, recovery can reconstruct the committed changes after a crash.
hint: Durability can come from the log.

front: What is the difference between an operation log and a physical data log?
back: An operation log records the logical action, while a physical log records byte- or page-level before/after changes.
accepted_answers: An operation log records the logical action, while a physical log records byte- or page-level before/after changes.
hint: Intent versus concrete data change.

front: What does a STEAL policy allow?
back: The buffer manager may flush a page containing uncommitted changes, so recovery must be able to undo those changes.
accepted_answers: The buffer manager may flush a page containing uncommitted changes, so recovery must be able to undo those changes.
hint: Uncommitted data may reach disk.

front: What does a NO-FORCE policy allow?
back: Commit does not require every changed page to be flushed immediately, so recovery must redo committed changes not yet on disk.
accepted_answers: Commit does not require every changed page to be flushed immediately, so recovery must redo committed changes not yet on disk.
hint: Committed pages may remain only in cache plus WAL.

front: Why do many systems combine STEAL and NO-FORCE?
back: The combination improves buffer flexibility and commit latency, while WAL-based undo and redo preserve correctness.
accepted_answers: The combination improves buffer flexibility and commit latency, while WAL-based undo and redo preserve correctness.
hint: Performance improves at the cost of recovery complexity.

front: What are the three broad phases of ARIES recovery?
back: Analysis, redo, and undo.
accepted_answers: Analysis, redo, and undo.
hint: Discover state, repeat history, roll back losers.

front: Why does ARIES redo history before undoing incomplete transactions?
back: Repeating logged actions reconstructs the exact pre-crash state, after which loser transactions can be rolled back consistently.
accepted_answers: Repeating logged actions reconstructs the exact pre-crash state, after which loser transactions can be rolled back consistently.
hint: Rebuild first, compensate second.

front: What is a compensation log record?
back: A log record describing an undo action so recovery remains restartable even if another crash happens during rollback.
accepted_answers: A log record describing an undo action so recovery remains restartable even if another crash happens during rollback.
hint: Undo work must itself be durable.

front: What does serializability guarantee?
back: The concurrent outcome is equivalent to some valid serial execution of the same transactions.
accepted_answers: The concurrent outcome is equivalent to some valid serial execution of the same transactions.
hint: Concurrent execution behaves like an order.

front: Why is serializability a property of the schedule rather than transaction code alone?
back: Individually correct transactions can still interfere; correctness depends on how their reads and writes interleave.
accepted_answers: Individually correct transactions can still interfere; correctness depends on how their reads and writes interleave.
hint: The interaction creates anomalies.

front: How does optimistic concurrency control work at a high level?
back: Transactions execute without holding long-lived write locks, then validate their read/write assumptions before committing.
accepted_answers: Transactions execute without holding long-lived write locks, then validate their read/write assumptions before committing.
hint: Work first, validate before publish.

front: When is optimistic concurrency control most attractive?
back: When conflicts are rare, because most transactions commit without lock waiting and little work is discarded.
accepted_answers: When conflicts are rare, because most transactions commit without lock waiting and little work is discarded.
hint: Low contention favors optimism.

front: How does pessimistic concurrency control differ?
back: It prevents conflicts up front by acquiring locks or otherwise restricting access before performing sensitive operations.
accepted_answers: It prevents conflicts up front by acquiring locks or otherwise restricting access before performing sensitive operations.
hint: Block risk instead of detecting it later.

front: How does MVCC reduce read-write blocking?
back: Readers can access a consistent older version while writers create newer versions, so they do not always contend for the same physical record.
accepted_answers: Readers can access a consistent older version while writers create newer versions, so they do not always contend for the same physical record.
hint: Different transactions can see different versions.

front: What new maintenance problem does MVCC introduce?
back: Obsolete row versions must be tracked and eventually reclaimed after no active transaction can still see them.
accepted_answers: Obsolete row versions must be tracked and eventually reclaimed after no active transaction can still see them.
hint: Version freedom creates cleanup work.

front: A production database shows high cache hit rate but poor latency. What should you investigate next?
back: Check latch contention, dirty-page flushing, WAL fsync latency, query plans, lock waits, and background maintenance; cache hits alone do not prove a fast request path.
accepted_answers: Check latch contention, dirty-page flushing, WAL fsync latency, query plans, lock waits, and background maintenance; cache hits alone do not prove a fast request path.
hint: One healthy metric cannot explain the whole path.
